statement_source_and_scope_match: SY10 defines the DAG and general white-box PIT question; KSS14 specifies the degree-at-every-gate convention and Q bit-complexity dependence. Unary d and binary constants make the customary polynomial-in-size-and-degree request explicit. This is the rational bounded-degree version; no equivalence with every field or arithmetic-network model is asserted.
proposed_statement_text:
An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates contain variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ or rational constants; every other gate has two inputs and applies addition or multiplication. Gates may feed more than one later gate. Operations take place in the ordinary commutative, associative polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$; subtraction can be implemented using the constant $-1$.

Let $L$ be the bit length of an explicit encoding of the graph, its gate labels and its rational constants, whose numerators and nonzero denominators are written in binary. The input also contains an integer $d\ge1$ in unary, with the promise that the polynomial computed at every gate has total degree at most $d$. The zero polynomial is permitted at any gate. Write $f_C$ for the output polynomial.

Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine $A$ and absolute constants $K,c>0$ such that, for every valid input $(C,d)$, $A$ uses at most $K(L+d)^c$ bit operations and correctly decides whether

$$
f_C\equiv0\quad\text{in }\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]?
$$

The machine receives the entire circuit and must work for all inputs satisfying the degree promise. There is no restriction on circuit depth, number of occurrences of a variable, or number of monomials. The conclusion is unconditional and requires no random choices. This is the rational-coefficient, bounded-degree, white-box version of polynomial identity testing (PIT).
applied_significance: Testing whether two symbolic computations are exactly equivalent reduces to applying PIT to their difference. Circuits retain shared intermediate computations and can describe polynomials whose expanded coefficient lists are exponentially larger. A deterministic polynomial-time test would give a worst-case guarantee for such identity checks without expanding the expressions. PIT also controls deterministic multivariate factorization when both the input polynomial and its factors are represented by circuits; the relevant reduction preserves this compact representation.

closest_existing_or_new_entries.difference: Matrix multiplication exponent asks arithmetic cost of computing a particular bilinear map, not zero-testing arbitrary symbolic circuits.
Explicit rigidity is a matrix construction/lower-bound question, not this universal decision algorithm.
Pseudospectral shattering concerns numerical perturbation and eigenvalue conditioning, not exact formal polynomial equality.
Log-rank controls communication while allowing unrestricted local computation; it is not a Turing-runtime PIT assertion.

open_status_evidence_summary: General ordinary commutative PIT remains explicitly unresolved in RMS25 §1 and ST26 §1; current searches and theorem comparisons found no matching unconditional polynomial-time result.
independent_status_corroboration: RMS25 authors are disjoint from SY10/KSS14/ST26; their introduction explicitly retains ordinary PIT as a major gap. Saxena S14 is a further independent survey.
strongest_known_partial_results_and_gap: Randomized polynomial-time testing is available. Representative recent deterministic advances include ST26 powering circuits and G26 three-term constant-bottom-degree circuits. AKT25 provides conditional general derandomization, not the hardness premise. No exhaustive ranking of all partial algorithms is claimed.

Bit-cost formulation must not be silently replaced by unit-cost arithmetic networks.
